text: Chapter five was about keeping inference running under varying load. Chapter six turns to the numbers underneath those decisions, starting with the most basic question: what does serving a token actually cost, and what makes that number move?

Cost per token comes from two numbers you already know: GPU dollars per hour, divided by sustained tokens-per-second throughput. Teams usually scale that up and report cost per million tokens, since a single token's cost is a tiny, hard-to-reason-about fraction of a cent.

Here's that formula as a few lines of Python — GPU hourly cost divided by tokens processed per hour, scaled to a cost per million tokens. With illustrative numbers, roughly two dollars an hour and two thousand tokens a second works out to about twenty-eight cents per million tokens.

That formula hides a trap: it assumes the GPU runs at that throughput continuously. A GPU costs the same per hour whether it's busy or idle, so a GPU running at twenty percent average utilization roughly multiplies the effective cost per token by five. Batching, smart autoscaling, and multi-model sharing all matter economically because every one of them raises sustained utilization.

Prefill and decode cost very different amounts for the same number of tokens. Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass, so it's cheap per token. Decode generates one token at a time, sequentially, which is why it dominates cost for long responses — and it's exactly why commercial APIs typically charge more per output token than per input token.

Cost per token comes from GPU price divided by sustained throughput, with utilization as the hidden multiplier and decode costing more than prefill. Up next, lesson thirty: you can't manage any of these numbers without first measuring them properly.
